demographics: About four times as many women as men are affected
More common in sexually active young women
Also common in older adults, especially those with urinary catheters or bladder emptying problems

risk_factors.text: Urinary catheter or recent instrumentation of the urinary tract
Urinary tract obstruction (stones, prostate enlargement, tumor)
Vesicoureteral reflux or other structural urinary tract abnormality

comorbidities: Neurogenic bladder or spinal cord injury
family_history: Vesicoureteral reflux or other congenital urinary tract anomaly
social_history: Recent hospitalization or residence in a long-term care facility

chief_complaints.text: I have to go to the bathroom all the time
I feel sick to my stomach

hpi.onset: Usually develops over several hours to a day, often after or alongside symptoms of a bladder infection
hpi.duration: Symptoms present for one to several days at presentation
hpi.progression: Urinary burning and frequency may precede or accompany the onset of fever and flank pain; symptoms build over hours to a day and then remain steady or worsen
hpi.location: One or both flanks, below the ribs and toward the back; may also have lower abdominal or suprapubic discomfort
hpi.radiation: Flank pain may radiate toward the groin or upper abdomen
hpi.quality: Constant, dull, aching or throbbing pain in the flank; burning with urination
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; flank pain often 6–8/10 and fever makes the patient feel very ill
hpi.timing: Continuous; chills may come in waves
aggravating: Pressing on the flank or back

associated_symptoms.text: Pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis

pertinent_negatives: Sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin (as with a kidney stone)
Pain that started before any urinary symptoms
Symptoms of septic shock such as confusion, fainting or very low blood pressure

negatives: Severe localized right lower quadrant pain

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, poor appetite or generalized weakness rather than fever and flank pain; fever may be blunted.
Infants and young children may have only fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or failure to thrive; older children may complain of abdominal pain rather than flank pain.
May present with preterm contractions, uterine tenderness or vague abdominal pain in addition to urinary symptoms; risk of preterm labor and low birth weight.
May have fewer localizing symptoms and progress rapidly to sepsis; fever may be absent or blunted.
Higher risk of severe infection, bacteremia and complications such as emphysematous pyelonephritis or renal abscess; symptoms may be less pronounced.
May have reduced urine output, fluid overload or electrolyte abnormalities; antibiotic dosing needs adjustment.

general.mild: Uncomfortable but not toxic; able to lie still, mild fatigue
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, flushed, prefers to lie still, grimaces with movement
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, rigors, reluctant to move
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, mottled, lethargic or confused, hypotensive

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not exclude pyelonephritis, especially in older or immunocompromised patients.
Rising creatinine suggests obstruction or acute kidney injury; adjust antibiotic dosing.
Elevated from dehydration, vomiting or reduced kidney function.
Elevated lactate with hypotension or organ dysfunction suggests sepsis from pyelonephritis.
Positive nitrite is fairly specific for a gram-negative urinary infection; a negative result does not rule it out.
White blood cell casts point to infection in the kidney rather than the bladder.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and before choosing antibiotics.

Leukocytosis with a left shift supports infection and helps gauge severity
Assesses kidney function, electrolytes and hydration before and during treatment
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and guides antibiotic choice

initial.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
initial.why: Defines complications such as obstruction, abscess or emphysematous pyelonephritis
initial.only_if: severe illness, suspected obstruction or abscess, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours of antibiotics

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for uncomplicated pyelonephritis that responds to antibiotics
not_indicated.only_if: severe illness, suspected obstruction or abscess, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours of antibiotics
pregnancy, renal impairment, suspected obstruction, or CT is not available

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management and does not show most stones
No role in the evaluation of flank pain or urinary infection
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected
Only if meningitis is suspected; not part of the pyelonephritis workup

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Ultrasound first in pregnancy, children and renal impairment; CT if complications are suspected
Blood cultures and lactate when sepsis is suspected
Image if there is no improvement after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics

differential.name: Kidney stone with obstruction or infection
differential.why_considered: Flank pain with nausea and vomiting is the classic presentation of both; a stone can also obstruct and cause pyelonephritis.
differential.trigger: Colicky pain that comes in waves and radiates to the groin, or a patient who is writhing and cannot lie still

history: Sudden onset of severe colicky pain
Pain radiates to the groin or testicle
Patient writhes and cannot get comfortable
Prior stone episodes
Pain started before any fever or urinary symptoms
exam: Costovertebral angle tenderness may be present but the patient is restless rather than lying still
No high fever at the start
labs: Leukocyte esterase and nitrite may be negative
White count usually normal unless infected

differential.name: Acute appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Right-sided abdominal pain with fever, nausea and vomiting can be mistaken for right pyelonephritis, especially in children and when the appendix is retrocecal.
differential.trigger: Pain that migrates from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant and localizes there

history: Periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant
Anorexia
Pain worsened by movement or coughing but not by urination
No dysuria or urinary frequency
exam: Right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding
Positive Rovsing, psoas or obturator signs
labs: Urinalysis usually bland; a few white cells can be seen if the appendix irritates the ureter
imaging: Enlarged, non-compressible appendix with surrounding fat stranding on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal or flank pain with a missed period in a patient who could be pregnant; can present with urinary symptoms and shock.
differential.trigger: Any patient of childbearing age with abdominal pain, especially with a missed period or vaginal bleeding

history: Missed period
Vaginal bleeding or spotting
Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain
Syncope or shoulder pain if ruptured
imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Fever, lower abdominal pain and dysuria in a sexually active young woman overlap with urinary tract infection.

history: Vaginal discharge
New or multiple sexual partners
Pain with intercourse
Bilateral lower abdominal pain
labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification test for gonorrhea or chlamydia
Urinalysis may show pyuria but nitrite is usually negative
imaging: Thickened fallopian tubes or free pelvic fluid on ultrasound

differential.name: Acute cholecystitis
differential.why_considered: Right upper quadrant or flank pain with fever, nausea and vomiting can be referred to the back and mimic right pyelonephritis.

history: Pain after fatty meals
Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder or scapula
No urinary symptoms
exam: Right upper quadrant tenderness with guarding
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin or transaminases
imaging: Gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid or sonographic Murphy sign on ultrasound

differential.name: Lower lobe pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Fever, chills and pleuritic pain referred to the upper abdomen or flank can be mistaken for pyelonephritis, especially in older adults.

history: Cough, sputum production or shortness of breath
Pleuritic chest pain worsened by deep breathing
No dysuria or urinary frequency
exam: Crackles, egophony or dullness at the lung base
labs: Hypoxemia on pulse oximetry or arterial blood gas
imaging: Lobar consolidation or infiltrate on chest x-ray or CT

differential.name: Musculoskeletal back pain
differential.why_considered: Flank and back pain are common reasons for presentation and can be confused with renal pain when urinary symptoms are mild.

history: Pain brought on by lifting, twisting or a fall
Pain worsened by specific movements and relieved by rest
No fever, chills or urinary symptoms
imaging: Normal kidneys on any imaging obtained
Degenerative changes or muscle spasm if spine imaged

severity.mild: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a stable, non-pregnant patient: low-grade fever, mild flank pain, able to eat and drink, no vomiting, normal kidney function, no signs of sepsis.
severity.moderate: Established uncomplicated pyelonephritis: fever above 100.4°F, moderate to severe flank pain, nausea or vomiting, leukocytosis, but hemodynamically stable and no organ dysfunction.
severity.severe: Complicated pyelonephritis: high fever with rigors, severe pain, vomiting preventing oral intake, suspected obstruction, abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis, or early sepsis with tachycardia and mild hypotension.
severity.critical: Septic shock from pyelonephritis: hypotension despite fluids, altered mental status, mottled skin, rising lactate, acute kidney injury, or respiratory failure; may also include emphysematous pyelonephritis or a ruptured renal abscess.

red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or septic shock; needs immediate fluids, cultures, IV antibiotics and likely ICU-level care
Sepsis with encephalopathy, especially in older adults; a poor prognostic sign
Tissue hypoperfusion; suggests sepsis and the need for aggressive resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Rising creatinine or decreasing urine output
red_flags.meaning: Acute kidney injury from obstruction, dehydration or sepsis; requires imaging and possible urinary drainage

red_flags.finding: Persistent fever or worsening pain after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Complicated infection such as obstruction, abscess or emphysematous pyelonephritis; needs imaging and possible drainage
Changes imaging and antibiotic choices and raises the risk of preterm labor and low birth weight

red_flags.finding: Immunocompromise or diabetes with severe infection
red_flags.meaning: Higher risk of bacteremia, abscess and emphysematous pyelonephritis; lower threshold for admission and imaging

complications.name: Renal or perinephric abscess
clues: Persistent fever after 48–72 hours of antibiotics
Fluid collection or mass on CT or ultrasound

complications.name: Emphysematous pyelonephritis
clues: Gas within the renal parenchyma on CT

complications.name: Papillary necrosis
clues: Diabetes, sickle cell disease or analgesic overuse
Flank pain with worsening renal function

complications.name: Chronic kidney disease or renal scarring
clues: Persistent creatinine elevation or scarring on imaging

special_populations.differences: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy is associated with preterm labor, low birth weight and maternal sepsis. Admit for IV antibiotics, obtain blood cultures, and use renal ultrasound first; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines.
May present with confusion, falls, poor appetite or generalized weakness rather than fever and flank pain. Fever may be blunted, and the risk of bacteremia and death is higher.

Infants and young children may have only fever, irritability, poor feeding or vomiting. Older children may complain of abdominal pain rather than flank pain. Obtain urine culture before antibiotics and image if there is a history of reflux or recurrent infection.
May have fewer localizing symptoms and progress rapidly to sepsis. Fever may be absent or blunted. Lower threshold for admission, blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Higher risk of severe infection, bacteremia, renal abscess and emphysematous pyelonephritis. Symptoms may be less pronounced. Image early if there is severe illness or failure to improve.
May have reduced urine output, fluid overload or electrolyte abnormalities. Adjust antibiotic doses for kidney function and avoid nephrotoxic agents when possible.

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and does it hurt when I tap on your back over the kidney area?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral flank pain below the ribs, worsened by percussion or movement

key_questions.question: When did the fever and flank pain start, and how quickly did they come on?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset over hours to a day, often after or alongside bladder symptoms

key_questions.question: Do you have burning, urgency or frequency when you urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Lower urinary tract symptoms preceding or accompanying the fever and flank pain

key_questions.question: Have you had chills or shaking chills?
Any nausea or vomiting, and can you keep fluids down?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting that prevents oral intake and may require IV fluids and admission

key_questions.question: Have you had a urinary catheter or any recent procedure on your urinary tract?
key_questions.looking_for: Catheter or instrumentation as a risk factor for complicated infection

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, kidney stones, an enlarged prostate, or any problem emptying your bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that predispose to obstruction, abscess or emphysematous pyelonephritis

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medicines that weaken your immune system, like prednisone or chemotherapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression that lowers the threshold for admission and broad-spectrum antibiotics

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, which changes imaging and antibiotic choices and raises the risk of preterm labor

key_questions.question: Any vaginal discharge, bleeding, or pain with intercourse?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or another gynecologic cause

key_questions.question: Have you had a kidney stone before, or pain that comes in waves and radiates to your groin?
key_questions.looking_for: Colicky radiating pain suggesting a stone rather than infection

key_questions.question: Any cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain when you breathe deeply?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests lower lobe pneumonia referred to the flank

key_questions.question: Have you felt confused, faint, or very weak?
key_questions.looking_for: Altered mental status or syncope suggesting sepsis or shock

Urinalysis with pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase and positive nitrite

Patient with right-sided pain and fever where appendicitis or cholecystitis is a strong alternative
